On an island of 100 perfectly logical people, all have blue eyes, but no one knows their own eye colour — there are no mirrors, and it is absolutely forbidden to discuss anyone's eye colour. Every person can see everyone else's eyes. The rule: if a person ever logically deduces with certainty that their own eyes are blue, they must leave the island at dawn the next day. One day a visitor publicly announces, in front of everyone simultaneously, 'At least one of you has blue eyes' — a fact every islander could already see was true just by looking around. After how many dawns do the blue-eyed islanders leave?
choices: The 100th dawn — the announcement, though it told no one anything they couldn't already see, creates common knowledge that triggers a chain of deduction taking exactly n dawns for n blue-eyed people
The 1st dawn — each person can already see 99 others with blue eyes, so they can deduce their own eyes are blue immediately
The 99th dawn, one day sooner than the number of blue-eyed people, since each person already excludes themselves from their own count
They never leave — the announcement provided no new information, since everyone already saw that others had blue eyes

questions.q: You bought a $60 non-refundable, non-transferable concert ticket. On the day of the show you feel sick, and would enjoy the concert only about half as much as usual — if the ticket had been free, you would definitely skip it tonight. From a purely rational, forward-looking standpoint, should the $60 you already spent affect tonight's decision to go?
choices: No, but only because concerts are non-transferable; a refundable ticket would change the answer
Yes, but only if the ticket cost more than $100
Yes — going recoups value from the money already spent, so you should go to avoid wasting it
No — the $60 is a sunk cost; it's already gone either way, so only tonight's expected enjoyment versus the cost of going tonight should matter

questions.q: A family sits on a porch on a hot day. Grandpa suggests driving 50 miles to a diner in Abilene for dinner. Each family member privately thinks it's a bad idea but assumes the others want to go, so everyone agrees to avoid seeming disagreeable. They drive, have a miserable, hot trip, and over dinner each admits they only went along because they thought everyone else wanted to. What is this phenomenon — where a group collectively agrees to a course of action that no individual member actually wants — called?
choices: The bystander effect — individuals fail to act because they assume someone else will
Social loafing — individuals exert less effort on a task when working as part of a group
Groupthink — the group suppresses dissent to preserve a false sense of harmony and overconfidence in its own judgment
The Abilene Paradox — a group agrees to a course of action that no individual member actually wants, because each person wrongly assumes the others want it

questions.q: Three voters rank three candidates as follows. Voter 1: A>B>C. Voter 2: B>C>A. Voter 3: C>A>B. In pairwise majority votes, A beats B 2-1, B beats C 2-1, and C beats A 2-1. What does this demonstrate about majority-rule voting with three or more options?
choices: The result proves A is the true winner, since A beats B and the cycle is just a tiebreaking artifact
One of the three pairwise vote counts must actually be a tie, so the cycle is only apparent

Majority-rule preferences can be cyclical even though every individual voter's own preferences are perfectly transitive — this is Condorcet's paradox, and it means there is no single 'majority winner' among the three candidates
A cycle like this can only happen with an even number of voters; three voters can never produce one

questions.q: In a two-day golf tournament, players who score far above the field average on day one tend, on average, to score closer to the field average on day two — even setting aside any psychological pressure of leading. What is the purely statistical explanation for this pattern?
choices: Regression to the mean — an extreme day-one score is partly luck, and luck (good or bad) tends not to repeat, so day-two scores drift back toward the average
The scoring must be measured incorrectly, since a player's true skill should produce the same score both days
This only happens because weaker players intentionally play more conservatively once they see they're ahead
Golf courses are deliberately made harder on the second day of tournaments to level the field
